positions/christian-nationalism-debates/: Christian nationalism (debates)
Christian nation ideology
Religious nationalism
Russkiy mir (Russian World) ideology (Orthodox form)

Advocates hold that a nation should be explicitly Christian in identity, law and public symbols, and that Christians should seek political power to that end; critics, many of them Christians, see this as idolatrous fusion of faith and nation.
Advocates: a nation’s heritage and laws are, or should be, grounded in Christianity, which should be publicly privileged.
Advocates: Christians have a duty to take dominion or exercise influence over government and culture (e.g. "Seven Mountains").
Advocates: secularism is not neutral but hostile to Christian moral order.
Critics: equating a nation with God’s people confuses the universal Church with ethnic or national identity and tends towards exclusion of minorities.
Psalm 33:12 ("Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD")
2 Chronicles 7:14
Matthew 28:19 ("disciple all nations")
Philippians 3:20
Galatians 3:28
Revelation 7:9

Draws on Constantinian and confessional-state traditions, Puritan covenant theology ("a city upon a hill", John Winthrop 1630), 19th-century "Christian America" movements and 20th-century Christian Reconstructionism (R. J. Rushdoony, 1973). Extreme historical forms include the Nazi-aligned "German Christians" (1930s) and Afrikaner Reformed justifications of apartheid. Contemporary debates involve the US (term popularised in scholarship by Whitehead and Perry, 2020; embraced by Stephen Wolfe, 2022), Russia’s "Russian World" ideology endorsed by Patriarch Kirill, Hungary, Brazil, Nigeria, Uganda and others.
R. J. Rushdoony (Christian Reconstructionism)
David Barton
Stephen Wolfe (The Case for Christian Nationalism, 2022)
Patriarch Kirill of Moscow ("Russian World")
Lance Wallnau (Seven Mountains)
Advocates argue that all law expresses some morality and every society has a public faith; Christians should not cede the public square to secular ideologies.
Many Western legal and moral traditions (human dignity, rule of law) historically derive from Christianity.
Scripture calls nations, not only individuals, to honour God (Ps 2; Matt 28:19).

Critics, including the Baptist Joint Committee’s "Christians Against Christian Nationalism" (2019), argue it betrays the Baptist and Christian heritage of religious liberty and the transnational nature of the Church.

Orthodox theologians’ Declaration on the "Russian World" Teaching (2022) condemned the fusion of Orthodoxy with Russian imperial nationalism used to justify the invasion of Ukraine as heresy (ethnophyletism, condemned by the Council of Constantinople in 1872).
History shows Christian nationalism sanctifying violence and racism (German Christians, apartheid), and sociological research links it to hostility toward minorities.
It confuses Israel’s unique covenant with modern nation-states.
Some advocates distinguish a benign "Christian heritage" patriotism or confessional-state ideal from racial or authoritarian nationalism.
They argue that critics often lump all public Christian advocacy (e.g. on abortion or marriage) under a pejorative label.
A major fault line in contemporary US evangelicalism and politics, especially since 2016.
Contributed to divisions within world Orthodoxy over the war in Ukraine.
Prompted renewed reflection on church, nation and religious liberty across the Global South.
positions/liberation-theology/altNames/1: Theology of the option for the poor
positions/liberation-theology/altNames/2: Black, Minjung, Dalit, feminist and Palestinian liberation theologies (related forms)
positions/liberation-theology/oneLine: God reveals himself as liberator of the oppressed, so theology must begin from the experience of the poor and commit the Church to transforming the unjust structures that oppress them.
positions/liberation-theology/coreClaims: Theology is "critical reflection on praxis" in the light of the Word, done from the standpoint of the poor.
God shows a preferential option for the poor, seen in the Exodus, the prophets and Jesus’ ministry (Luke 4:18).
Sin is personal and also structural ("institutionalised violence", social sin).
Salvation embraces liberation from social, economic and political oppression as well as from sin, in one history.
Base ecclesial communities read Scripture together and act for justice.
positions/liberation-theology/origin: Emerged in Latin America in the 1960s amid poverty, dictatorships and Vatican II’s openness. The Medellín conference of Latin American bishops (1968) denounced "institutionalised violence"; Gustavo Gutiérrez’s A Theology of Liberation (1971) gave it its name. Parallel movements: James Cone’s Black Theology and Black Power (1969), Korean Minjung theology (1970s), Dalit theology in India, Palestinian theology (Naim Ateek), South African contextual theology (Kairos Document, 1985) and feminist theology.
positions/liberation-theology/strongestA: The Exodus, the prophets and Jesus’ Nazareth manifesto (Luke 4:18) show God’s concern for the oppressed as central, not peripheral.
Theology has always been shaped by social location; liberation theology makes this explicit and gives voice to the poor majority of Christians.
It inspired heroic witness, including martyrs such as Romero and the Jesuits of the UCA in El Salvador (1989).
Catholic social teaching itself adopted the "preferential option for the poor" (Puebla 1979; John Paul II; Francis).
positions/liberation-theology/strongestO: The Vatican’s Libertatis Nuntius (1984) warned that uncritical borrowing of Marxist class analysis distorts the gospel and the Church.
Critics argue it reduces salvation to political liberation, neglecting personal sin, forgiveness and eternal life.
Evangelical and Pentecostal growth among Latin America’s poor suggests many of the poor themselves opted for other forms of faith.
Some liberation movements were associated with armed revolution, contrary to gospel nonviolence.
positions/liberation-theology/responses/: Gutiérrez stressed that liberation has three levels (social, personal, and liberation from sin into communion with God) and that Marxism was a tool of analysis, not a faith.
The CDF’s second instruction (Libertatis Conscientia, 1986) affirmed authentic Christian liberation, and later popes embraced the option for the poor.
positions/liberation-theology/consequenc: Transformed Latin American Catholicism and influenced global Christian social ethics.
Led to persecution and martyrdom of clergy and catechists under military regimes.
Provoked Vatican discipline (e.g. silencing of Leonardo Boff, 1985) and later reconciliation.
Inspired contextual theologies across Africa, Asia and among minorities in the West.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/oneLine: Historically, many Christians, especially in the antebellum American South and in colonial empires, argued that Scripture sanctioned the enslavement of Africans; this theology is today repudiated by virtually all churches as a grave betrayal of the gospel.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/coreClaim: (Historically argued) The patriarchs owned slaves and the Mosaic law regulated slavery, so it cannot be intrinsically sinful.
(Historically argued) Jesus never condemned slavery, and the apostles told slaves to obey their masters and returned the runaway Onesimus.
(Historically argued) The "curse of Ham" (Gen 9:25, actually a curse on Canaan) justified African servitude, a reading with no basis in the text.
(Historically argued) A paternalist order of master and slave, with Christian instruction of the enslaved, was a divinely ordained social hierarchy.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/origin: Medieval and early modern Christians widely accepted slavery; papal bulls Dum Diversas (1452) and Romanus Pontifex (1455) authorised the Portuguese to enslave "Saracens and pagans". As abolitionism grew, American theologians developed explicit biblical defences: Richard Furman’s Exposition (1823), Thornton Stringfellow (1841), James Henley Thornwell, Robert L. Dabney, Frederick A. Ross (Slavery Ordained of God, 1857) and Benjamin M. Palmer (1860). Recorded here historically and critically.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/proponent: Many colonial-era clergy across Catholic and Protestant empires
positions/pro-slavery-theology/strongest: (As its defenders argued) Scripture nowhere explicitly abolishes slavery and the apostles regulated it within Christian households; abolitionists, they claimed, set human reason above the Bible.
(As its defenders argued) Rejecting slavery’s biblical regulation would undermine the authority of Scripture generally, a hermeneutical worry that made the debate a "theological crisis" (Noll).

(As its defenders argued) Social order and Christian mission to the enslaved required stable hierarchy. Historians note that these arguments persuaded many sincere believers, which is why they must be studied honestly rather than ignored.
Scripture condemns "manstealing" with death (Exodus 21:16) and lists "menstealers" among the lawless (1 Tim 1:10), which describes the Atlantic slave trade exactly.
All humans bear God’s image (Gen 1:27), and in Christ there is "neither bond nor free" (Gal 3:28); Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus "not now as a servant ... but a brother beloved".
Hebrew debt-servitude, with release in the seventh year and Jubilee and protection of runaways (Deut 23:15–16), was fundamentally unlike hereditary, race-based chattel slavery.

The "curse of Ham" reading is exegetically baseless (the curse falls on Canaan and says nothing of race), and enslaved Christians (Douglass, spirituals, Black churches) exposed the system’s contradiction of the gospel.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/responses: Pro-slavery writers historically replied that the "spirit" of Scripture could not override its "letter", and accused abolitionists of infidelity.

Modern historians and theologians respond that the episode demonstrates how interpreters’ social interests can distort exegesis, and the Southern Baptist Convention (1995), PCUSA and others have formally repented of their predecessors’ defence of slavery and racism.
positions/pro-slavery-theology/consequen: Split the Methodist (1844), Baptist (1845) and Presbyterian churches along North–South lines.
Gave religious legitimacy to the Confederacy and later to segregation ("Jim Crow") theology.
Left a lasting legacy of racial division in American Christianity and a cautionary example in hermeneutics.
Formally repented of by the denominations that once taught it.
positions/abolitionism/oneLine: Slavery and the slave trade are sins against God and the image of God in every person, and Christians must work for their abolition.
positions/abolitionism/coreClaims/0: All humans are made in God’s image and of "one blood" (Acts 17:26).
positions/abolitionism/coreClaims/1: Manstealing is a capital crime in Scripture (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10), and the golden rule forbids holding others in bondage.
positions/abolitionism/coreClaims/2: In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Gal 3:28); the gospel’s logic undermines slavery.
positions/abolitionism/coreClaims/3: Christian love requires political action to end the trade and emancipate the enslaved.
positions/abolitionism/origin: Gregory of Nyssa’s Fourth Homily on Ecclesiastes (c.379) condemned slaveholding outright, a rare ancient voice. Bartolomé de las Casas defended indigenous Americans’ freedom (1540s–50s). Organised abolitionism began with Quakers (Germantown Protest, 1688; John Woolman; Anthony Benezet), joined by Methodists (Wesley’s Thoughts upon Slavery, 1774), Anglican evangelicals (William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp; Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade, 1787), African Christians (Olaudah Equiano), Black churches (Richard Allen) and American evangelicals and revivalists (Charles Finney’s Oberlin).
positions/abolitionism/proponentsOther/9: Pope Gregory XVI (In Supremo Apostolatus, 1839, condemning the slave trade)
positions/abolitionism/strongestArgument: It applies the Bible’s deepest principles (image of God, love of neighbour, redemption from bondage in the Exodus) rather than isolated regulations of an ancient institution.
It was vindicated by the testimony of the enslaved themselves and by the fruits of emancipation.
Its leaders combined evangelical faith with practical political strategy, achieving one of history’s great moral reforms.
positions/abolitionism/strongestObjectio: In its own day, pro-slavery critics argued that abolitionists ignored explicit biblical regulation of slavery (a hermeneutical objection that troubled even some anti-slavery theologians such as Charles Hodge).
Some radical abolitionists rejected scriptural authority or the churches altogether, confirming conservative fears.
Historians note that British abolition coexisted with colonial expansion, and that "legitimate commerce" and anti-slavery could justify imperial intervention in Africa.
positions/abolitionism/responses/0: Abolitionists answered that Scripture must be read as a whole and in light of Christ, and that New Testament slavery was not race-based chattel slavery.
positions/abolitionism/responses/1: African Christian leaders such as Samuel Ajayi Crowther, himself freed from a slave ship in 1822, show abolition and African agency combined in mission.
positions/abolitionism/consequences/0: Abolition of the British slave trade (1807) and of slavery in British colonies (1834), the US (1865) and Brazil (1888).
positions/abolitionism/consequences/1: Founded settlements for freed people (Sierra Leone, 1787/1792) that became centres of West African Christianity.
positions/abolitionism/consequences/2: Created models for Christian social reform movements thereafter.
